items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the contrast of an X-ray image of soft tissue can be improved. (b) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of a CT scan compared with a single X-ray image.
items.answer: (a) Use a contrast medium with a high attenuation coefficient (e.g. barium or iodine) in the organ, or use lower-energy (softer) X-rays where absorption differences are greater. (b) Advantages: 3D image, distinguishes overlapping structures and soft tissues with small attenuation differences. Disadvantage: much larger radiation dose (and cost, time).
items.markingKey: (a) contrast medium (barium/iodine) [1]; reason: high μ / greater difference [1] [2] (b) advantage [1]; disadvantage (dose) [1] [2]

items.stem: A 2.0 kg block of brass is heated by a 60 W heater inserted in a hole in the block. A thermometer is placed in a second hole. (a) Define specific heat capacity. (b) The specific heat capacity of brass is 380 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the rate of rise of temperature in K per minute, assuming no losses. (c) Describe how the heater power would be measured. (d) Explain why the measured rate of temperature rise is less than the calculated value. (e) Explain why the temperature continues to rise briefly after the heater is switched off.
items.answer: (a) Energy per unit mass needed to raise the temperature by 1 K. (b) 4.74 K min⁻¹ (c) Ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel with the heater; P = VI. (d) Energy is lost to the surroundings and used to heat the heater and thermometer. (e) The heater is hotter than the block and continues to transfer energy to it.
items.markingKey: (a) Energy per unit mass needed to raise the temperature by 1 K [1] (b) Δθ/t = P/(mc) × 60 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.74 K min⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (c) ammeter and voltmeter [1]; P = VI [1] [2] (d) Energy is lost to the surroundings and used to heat the heater and thermometer [1] (e) The heater is hotter than the block and continues to transfer energy to it [1]

items.stem: Jupiter may be treated as a uniform sphere of radius 6.99 × 10⁷ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 25.9 N kg⁻¹. (a) State Newton's law of gravitation. items.answer: (a) Force between point masses ∝ product of masses and ∝ 1/separation². (b) M = gR²/G = 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg (c) 2.88 N kg⁻¹

items.stem: An electromagnet used in a scrapyard in Manila consists of a solenoid carrying 3.0 A wound on an iron core. (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern inside and outside the solenoid. (b) State two ways to increase the field strength. (c) Explain how to identify which end is the north pole. (d) Describe the force between two adjacent turns of the coil.
items.answer: (a) Inside: uniform, parallel to the axis. Outside: like a bar magnet, lines from N end round to S end. (b) Increase the current; increase turns per unit length; insert an iron core. (c) Right-hand grip rule: fingers in the direction of the current, thumb points to the N pole (or view from the end: anticlockwise = N). (d) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract.
items.markingKey: (a) inside uniform [1]; outside bar-magnet pattern [1] [2] (b) first way [1]; second way [1] [2] (c) Right-hand grip rule: fingers in the direction of the current, thumb points to the N pole (or view from the end: anticlockwise = N) [1] (d) Adjacent turns carry current in the same direction, so they attract [1]

items.stem: 0.50 kg of water at 100 °C in a kettle is boiled until it has all turned to steam at 100 °C. (a) Define internal energy. items.answer: (a) Sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules. (b) Unchanged: the temperature is constant. (c) 1.13 × 10⁶ J (d) Some energy is used to do work pushing back the atmosphere as the steam expands (W = pΔV).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Derive the expression V_H = BI/(ntq) for the Hall voltage across a slice of width d and thickness t. (b) Explain how a Hall probe must be oriented to measure the flux density of a field.
items.answer: (a) At equilibrium qV_H/d = Bqv, so V_H = Bvd. With I = nAvq and A = dt, v = I/(ndtq). So V_H = BId/(ndtq) = BI/(ntq). (b) The probe face must be perpendicular to the field lines (field perpendicular to the current in the slice), so that the full BQv acts; rotate until the Hall voltage is maximum.
items.markingKey: (a) qV_H/d = Bqv [1]; substitute v = I/(nAq) with A = dt [1] [2] (b) field perpendicular to slice / current [1]; maximum reading [1] [2]

items.stem: An atom has three energy levels at −10.4 eV, −5.5 eV and −0.90 eV. (a) State the number of different photon energies that can be emitted. (b) Calculate the largest photon energy emitted, in joules. (c) Calculate the longest wavelength emitted. (d) Explain why the energy levels are negative. (e) Explain the difference between an emission and an absorption spectrum.
items.answer: (a) 3 (b) 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (c) 2.70 × 10⁻⁷ m (d) Zero is the energy of an electron just free of the atom; bound electrons have less energy. (e) Emission: bright lines from excited atoms; absorption: dark lines in a continuous spectrum where cool atoms absorb photons of the same energies.
items.markingKey: (a) three transitions: 3 [1] (b) ΔE × e (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.52 × 10⁻¹⁸ J [1] [2] (c) smallest ΔE, λ = hc/ΔE (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.70 × 10⁻⁷ m [1] [2] (d) Zero is the energy of an electron just free of the atom; bound electrons have less energy [1] (e) emission bright lines [1]; absorption dark lines in continuum [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how Hubble's law supports the Big Bang theory. (b) Explain why it does not mean that the Earth is at the centre of the Universe when all distant galaxies are seen to be moving away from us.
items.answer: (a) All distant galaxies are receding with speeds proportional to their distances, so the Universe is expanding; tracing the expansion back in time implies that everything was once concentrated at a single point and has been expanding since. items.stem: A 10 000 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V and then used to lift a small mass with an electric motor. (a) Calculate the charge stored. (b) Calculate the energy stored. (c) The motor is 20% efficient. Calculate the maximum height to which it can lift a 50 g mass. (d) Explain why the energy stored is ½QV, not QV.
items.answer: (a) 0.12 C (b) 0.72 J (c) 0.294 m (d) The p.d. rises from zero during charging, so the average p.d. against which charge is moved is ½V.
items.markingKey: (a) Q = CV: 0.12 C [1] (b) W = ½CV² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.72 J with unit [1] [2] (c) mgh = 0.2W (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.294 m with unit [1] [2] (d) The p.d. rises from zero during charging, so the average p.d. against which charge is moved is ½V [1]

items.stem: An electron moves at 1.5 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 1.2 T. (a) Calculate the magnetic force on it. (b) Explain why its kinetic energy does not change. (c) State the effect on the force of doubling the speed.
items.answer: (a) 1.44 × 10⁻¹³ N (b) the force is perpendicular to the velocity, so no work is done (c) the force doubles
items.markingKey: (a) F = BQv sin θ [1]; = 1.44 × 10⁻¹³ N [1] (b) force ⊥ velocity, no work [1] (c) doubles (F ∝ v) [1] [4]

items.stem: A fusion reaction is ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n. Data: nuclear masses: ²₁H 2.013553 u, ³₁H 3.015501 u, ³₂He 3.014932 u, ⁴₂He 4.001506 u, ¹₀n 1.008665 u, ¹₁p 1.007276 u. Calculate the energy released in the reaction in MeV.
items.answer: 3.28 MeV
items.markingKey: Δm = 0.003509 u [1]; E = Δmc² with Δm in kg [1]; = 3.28 MeV [1] [3]

items.stem: A technician in Hanoi calibrates a freezer thermometer. (a) State what is meant by thermal equilibrium. (b) Explain why the thermodynamic scale is called an absolute scale. (c) Explain why a temperature change of 10 °C equals a change of 10 K.
items.answer: (a) No net transfer of thermal energy between two bodies (they are at the same temperature). (b) It does not depend on the property of any substance and its zero is absolute zero. (c) The kelvin and the degree Celsius are the same size; the scales only differ in their zero.
items.markingKey: (a) No net transfer of thermal energy between two bodies (they are at the same temperature) [1] (b) independent of substance [1]; zero at absolute zero [1] [2] (c) same size of degree [1]; offset of 273.15 [1] [2]

items.stem: An oscilloscope displays a sinusoidal trace. The time-base is 5.0 ms div⁻¹ and the Y-gain is 5.0 V div⁻¹. One complete cycle occupies 2.5 divisions horizontally, and the trace extends 1.5 divisions above and below the centre line. Determine the period, the frequency and the peak voltage.
items.markingKey: T = divisions × time-base = 12.5 ms [1]; f = 1/T = 80 Hz [1]; V₀ = 1.5 × 5.0 = 7.5 V [1] [3]

items.stem: Why is the energy stored in a capacitor ½QV rather than QV?
options: the p.d. increases from zero as the charge is added, so the average p.d. is ½V
half the energy is always lost as heat in the capacitor
the charge on each plate is ½Q
items.answer: the p.d. increases from zero as the charge is added, so the average p.d. is ½V
items.markingKey: Each increment of charge is moved against the p.d. at that moment.

items.stem: Why is the thermodynamic scale described as an absolute scale?
options: It is the scale used by all thermometers
It uses the melting point of ice as its zero
It can never have negative values for any substance
It does not depend on the property of any particular substance
items.answer: It does not depend on the property of any particular substance
items.markingKey: It is defined theoretically, with zero at absolute zero.

items.stem: Explain why a wine glass can be shattered by a loud note of one particular pitch.
items.answer: The note's frequency equals the natural frequency of the glass; resonance gives a large-amplitude vibration that strains the glass beyond breaking.
items.markingKey: identifies resonance or damping correctly [1]; links frequency/energy transfer to the effect [1] [2]

items.stem: 25 g of water at 100 °C is boiled in an open pan in a kitchen in Accra at atmospheric pressure (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa) to form steam at 100 °C. The density of the water is 1000 kg m⁻³ and of the steam 0.60 kg m⁻³. (specific latent heat of vaporisation 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹) What is the thermal energy supplied?

A bridge rectifier is connected to a 50 Hz supply of peak voltage 12 V (ignore p.d.s across the diodes). The output is connected to a 5.0 kΩ load with a 220 μF capacitor in parallel. (a) State the purpose of the four diodes. (b) Describe the output without the capacitor. (c) Calculate the ripple voltage, assuming discharge for 10 ms between peaks.
items.answer: (a) Full-wave rectification: current through the load in one direction in both half-cycles. (b) Half-sine pulses, all positive, 100 per second, peak 12 V. (c) 0.109 V
items.markingKey: (a) Full-wave rectification: current through the load in one direction in both half-cycles [1] (b) all positive pulses [1]; 100 Hz [1] [2] (c) V₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)) (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 0.109 V with unit [1] [3]

items.stem: A horizontal copper rod of mass 3.0 g and length 5.0 cm lies at right angles to a horizontal uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.60 T. (a) Calculate the current needed for the magnetic force to support the weight of the rod. (b) State how the direction of the current must be chosen. (c) Calculate the force on the rod if the current is 4.5 A and the rod is turned to 30° to the field.
items.answer: (a) 0.981 A (b) so that Fleming's left-hand rule gives an upward force (c) 0.0675 N
items.markingKey: (a) BIL = mg [1]; I = 0.981 A [1] (b) FLHR, force upwards [1] (c) F = BIL sin θ [1]; = 0.0675 N [1] [5]

items.stem: A research hospital in Manila injects a patient with a tracer labelled with carbon-11, which decays by β⁺ emission with a half-life of 20.4 minutes. (a) Write the decay equation for carbon-11. (b) Describe what happens to the positron emitted. (c) Calculate the energy of each annihilation photon in MeV. (d) Calculate the fraction of the tracer remaining after 40.8 minutes. (e) Explain why the tracer must be produced close to the hospital.
items.answer: (a) ¹¹₆C → ¹¹₅B + ⁰₊₁e + ν (b) It travels a very short distance in tissue and annihilates with an electron, producing two γ-photons in opposite directions. (c) 0.512 MeV (d) 0.25 (e) Its short half-life means it would decay significantly during transport.
items.markingKey: (a) products correct [1]; neutrino [1] [2] (b) annihilates with electron [1]; two photons opposite [1] [2] (c) E = mₑc² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.512 MeV with unit [1] [2] (d) 2 half-lives: 0.25 [1] (e) Its short half-life means it would decay significantly during transport [1]

items.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 300 nm is shone onto a sodium plate (work function 2.3 eV) connected to a sensitive ammeter circuit. (a) Calculate the threshold wavelength. (b) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (c) State and explain the effect on Ek(max) of doubling the intensity. (d) Explain why the electrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies.
items.answer: (a) 540 nm (b) 2.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (c) No change: photon energy unchanged. (d) Electrons from below the surface lose energy in escaping; only surface electrons have Ek(max).
items.markingKey: (a) λ₀ = hc/Φ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 540 nm with unit [1] [2] (b) hf − Φ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ J [1] [2] (c) No change: photon energy unchanged [1] (d) Electrons from below the surface lose energy in escaping; only surface electrons have Ek(max) [1]

items.stem: In a simple model of the hydrogen atom, an electron orbits a proton in a circle of radius 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m. (a) Calculate the electric force between the electron and the proton. (b) Calculate the electric field strength due to the proton at the electron. (c) Calculate the speed of the electron, assuming the electric force provides the centripetal force.
items.markingKey: (a) F = e²/(4πε₀r²) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 8.19 × 10⁻⁸ N [1] [2] (b) E = e/(4πε₀r²) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.12 × 10¹¹ N C⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) F = mv²/r (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.18 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: The mass of a ¹²₆C nucleus is 11.996709 u. The mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). (a) Calculate the mass defect in u. (b) Calculate the binding energy in MeV. (c) Calculate the binding energy per nucleon.
A measured value is 25 ± 1.0. Calculate lg of the value and its absolute uncertainty, giving both to an appropriate number of decimal places.
items.markingKey: lg x = 1.398 [1]; uncertainty = 0.017 [1]; consistent decimal places [1] [3]

items.stem: A roller-coaster car of mass 600 kg is released from rest at a height of 40 m above the bottom of a vertical circular loop of radius 8.0 m. Friction is negligible. (a) Calculate the speed of the car at the top of the loop. (b) Calculate the normal contact force at the bottom of the loop.
items.markingKey: (a) mg(h − 2r) = ½mv² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 21.7 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) N − mg = mv²/r with v² = 2gh (equation) [1]; substitution [1]; answer 64 700 N with unit [1] [3]

items.stem: A circular coil of diameter 8.0 cm has 500 turns and is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.30 T. Calculate the area of the coil, the flux through one turn and the flux linkage.
What provides the centripetal force on the Moon as it orbits the Earth?
options: the Moon's weight towards the Sun
the gravitational pull of the Earth
items.answer: the gravitational pull of the Earth
items.markingKey: Gravity acts towards the Earth's centre.

items.stem: Which describes critical damping?
options: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating
the system returns very slowly without oscillating
the amplitude decreases slowly over many oscillations
the system oscillates with increasing amplitude
items.answer: the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating
items.markingKey: Critical damping: fastest return, no overshoot.

items.stem: A cup of tea at 70 °C is placed in contact with a swimming pool at 26 °C. A student says thermal energy will flow into the hotter object because the other has more internal energy. Explain why the student is wrong and describe what happens until thermal equilibrium is reached.
items.answer: Net thermal energy flows from higher to lower temperature, i.e. from a cup of tea at 70 °C to a swimming pool at 26 °C, regardless of internal energy, until both reach the same temperature, after which there is no net transfer.
items.markingKey: direction set by temperature not internal energy [1]; flow from hotter to colder [1] [2]

items.stem: Venus has mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m. What is the gravitational potential at the surface of Venus?

In an electron diffraction tube, electrons are accelerated through 3000 V and pass through a thin layer of graphite. Concentric rings are seen on a fluorescent screen. (a) Explain how the rings show that electrons behave as waves. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron. (c) Calculate the momentum of an electron. (d) State and explain the effect on the rings of increasing the accelerating voltage.
items.answer: (a) Rings are a diffraction pattern, which is a wave property. (b) 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁶ J (c) 2.96 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ (d) Rings get smaller: higher p gives smaller λ, so less diffraction.
items.markingKey: (a) Rings are a diffraction pattern, which is a wave property [1] (b) Ek = eV: 4.80 × 10⁻¹⁶ J [1] (c) p = √(2mEk) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.96 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (d) rings smaller [1]; larger p, smaller λ, less diffraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Data from an experiment (t / s, V / V): t = 0, V = 12; t = 10, V = 7.28; t = 20, V = 4.41; t = 30, V = 2.68; t = 40, V = 1.62; t = 50, V = 0.985. (a) Explain why a graph of the natural logarithm of the second quantity against the first should be a straight line. (b) Determine the gradient of this graph. (c) The resistance is 47 kΩ. Calculate the capacitance.
items.answer: (a) exponential decay y = y₀e^(−kx) gives ln y = ln y₀ − kx (b) −5.00 × 10⁻² (in units of s⁻¹) C = RC/R = 4.26 × 10⁻⁴ F
items.markingKey: (a) ln y = ln y₀ − kx linear [1] (b) ln values [1]; gradient = −5.00 × 10⁻² [1] (c) RC = −1/gradient = 20 s [1]; C = 4.26 × 10⁻⁴ F [1] [5]

items.stem: A PET centre in Nairobi injects a patient with a tracer labelled with nitrogen-13, which decays by β⁺ emission with a half-life of 9.97 minutes. (a) Write the decay equation for nitrogen-13. (b) Describe what happens to the positron emitted. (c) Calculate the energy of each annihilation photon in MeV. (d) The two photons from one annihilation arrive at opposite detectors 0.30 ns apart. Calculate the distance of the annihilation from the midpoint between the detectors.
items.answer: (a) ¹³₇N → ¹³₆C + ⁰₊₁e + ν (b) It travels a very short distance in tissue and annihilates with an electron, producing two γ-photons in opposite directions. (c) 0.512 MeV (d) 4.5 cm
items.markingKey: (a) products correct [1]; neutrino [1] [2] (b) annihilates with electron [1]; two photons opposite [1] [2] (c) E = mₑc² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.512 MeV with unit [1] [2] (d) cΔt/2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.5 cm with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: An energy researcher in Lisbon compares the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number, which rises steeply to a peak of about 8.8 MeV near A = 56 and falls to about 7.56 MeV for plutonium-239. (a) Define binding energy per nucleon. (b) Explain, using the graph, why fission of plutonium-239 releases energy. (c) Estimate the energy released when a plutonium-239 nucleus splits into two nuclei each with BE per nucleon 8.5 MeV (ignore free neutrons). (d) Explain why iron-56 cannot release energy by fission or fusion.
items.answer: (a) Total binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons. (b) The products (A ≈ 90–140) have higher BE per nucleon (≈ 8.5 MeV) than plutonium-239 (7.56 MeV), so total BE increases. (c) 225 MeV (d) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input.
items.markingKey: (a) Total binding energy of a nucleus divided by the number of nucleons [1] (b) products higher BE per nucleon [1]; total BE increases, energy released [1] [2] (c) 239 × (8.5 − 7.56) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 225 MeV with unit [1] [2] (d) It is at the peak; any change gives nuclei with lower BE per nucleon, which would require energy input [1]

items.stem: The dome of a Van de Graaff generator in a Hanoi science museum is a sphere of radius 10 cm at a potential of 2.0 × 10⁵ V. (a) Define electric potential at a point. (b) Calculate the charge on the dome. (c) Calculate the field strength at the surface of the dome.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit positive charge bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point. (b) 2.22 × 10⁻⁶ C (c) 2.00 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) work per unit charge [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) Q = 4πε₀RV (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.22 × 10⁻⁶ C [1] [2] (c) E = V/R for a sphere (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.00 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: The output of a full-wave rectifier connected to a 60 Hz supply has a peak value of 15 V. A 220 μF smoothing capacitor is connected across a 1.0 kΩ load. Assume the capacitor discharges through the load for the whole interval between peaks. (a) Calculate the time between peaks. (b) Calculate the minimum p.d. across the load. (c) Calculate the peak-to-peak ripple voltage and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) 8.33 ms (b) 14.4 V (c) 0.558 V; use a larger capacitance (or full-wave rectification / larger load resistance)
items.markingKey: (a) 8.33 ms [1] (b) V = V₀e^(−t/RC) [1]; 14.4 V [1] (c) ripple = 0.558 V [1]; valid improvement [1] [5]

items.stem: A container holds 1.0 mol of an ideal monatomic gas at 300 K. The gas is heated to 320 K. Calculate the increase in internal energy and explain why the gas has no intermolecular potential energy.
items.answer: ΔU = 249 J; ideal gas has no intermolecular forces
items.markingKey: U = (3/2)nRT [1]; ΔU = 1.5nRΔT = 249 J [1]; no forces between molecules [1] [3]

items.stem: Observations of Spica show that its spectrum peaks at 1.29 × 10⁻⁷ m and that its luminosity is 7.85 × 10³⁰ W. (a) Calculate the surface temperature. (b) State one assumption made in these calculations. (c) Calculate the power emitted per unit area of its surface.
items.answer: (a) 22 400 K (b) The star is a black body (or a uniform sphere). (c) 1.43 × 10¹⁰ W m⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) T = 2.9 × 10⁻³/λmax (method/substitution) [1]; answer 22 400 K with unit [1] [2] (b) The star is a black body (or a uniform sphere) [1] (c) σT⁴ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.43 × 10¹⁰ W m⁻² [1] [2]

items.stem: In a model, the molecules of a gas have speeds of 400, 600, 700, 800, 900 m s⁻¹. Calculate the mean speed, the mean-square speed and the root-mean-square speed.
items.answer: mean = 680 m s⁻¹; ⟨c²⟩ = 4.92 × 10⁵ m² s⁻²; c_rms = 701 m s⁻¹
